sentences.text: Dyslocosaurus was a sauropod dinosaur similar to Diplodocus but smaller in size.
This animal reached lengths of 18 meters, heights of 4.5 meters, and weighed approximately 6 tons.
It was characterized by having four, possibly five, clawed toes, whereas diplodocids typically have three.
The species name polyonychius means "many-clawed" and refers to the unusual number of claws on the foot.
The genus name Dyslocosaurus means "hard-to-place lizard" and refers to the scarcity of data about the fossil's original location.
The fossil remains of Dyslocosaurus were collected by Professor Frederic Brewster Loomis.
The only known location for the Dyslocosaurus fossil is Lance Creek, a county in east Wyoming.
The type specimen of Dyslocosaurus, catalog number AC 663, is housed in the Amherst College Museum of Natural History.
John Stanton McIntosh, William Coombs, and Dale Russell described Dyslocosaurus as a new genus and species in 1992.
The original describers interpreted the limb bones of Dyslocosaurus as belonging to a diplodocid dinosaur.
Dyslocosaurus is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae.
It belongs to the superfamily Diplodocoidea.
Dyslocosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic Period, approximately 150 to 147 million years ago, in what is now North America.
The time range for Dyslocosaurus is estimated from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
In 1998, Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson proposed that the Dyslocosaurus specimen was actually a chimera mixing titanosaur limb bones and theropod phalanges from the Lance Formation.
In 2015, Tschopp et al. raised doubts about whether Dyslocosaurus had more than three claws, noting that one pedal bone in the specimen differed in preservation and color from the others.
Some analyses have recovered Dyslocosaurus as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae, potentially making it the second dicraeosaurid known from North America.
